findings.title: Max-count cleanup can delete annotations that moved into the retained set
findings.body: The IDs are selected using the max-count offset, then deleted in a separate statement without rechecking their rank. If another request deletes a newer annotation between those statements, a selected ID can move into the set that should be retained but will still be deleted. For example, with a max count of 1, cleanup selects the older of two annotations; if a user deletes the newer one before this delete, cleanup then removes the only remaining annotation.

findings.title: Building SQLite ID lists with repeated formatting has quadratic cost
findings.body: Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string with `fmt.Sprintf`, so constructing the IN-list takes quadratic time and allocation in the number of IDs. The added test exercises this path with batches containing over 13,000 IDs, causing hundreds of megabytes of cumulative string allocations per list; larger configured batches can impose substantial CPU and GC pressure on cleanup.

findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with every ID
findings.body: This logs each batch at error level and includes the full ID list even when the query succeeded; the subsequent delete log does the same. Normal cleanup therefore produces error-level log entries and potentially very large log messages for every batch, creating alert noise and avoidable log-volume overhead.
